name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q01 - Physical equilibria and constant parameters

questiontext.text:
Match the physical equilibrium processes with their corresponding constant parameters at equilibrium.

List I (Process)List II (Constant Parameter)
(A) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})\)(1) Melting point is fixed at constant pressure
(B) \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\)(2) \(p_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}}\) is constant at a given temperature
(C) \(\text{Sugar}(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Sugar}(\text{solution})\)(3) \(\frac{[\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{aq})]}{[\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})]}\) is constant at a given temperature
(D) \(\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{aq})\)(4) Concentration of solute in solution is constant at a given temperature

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Every physical equilibrium in a closed system at a given temperature is characterized by a constant measurable parameter.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Process
For the liquid-vapour equilibrium \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})\), the equilibrium vapour pressure \(p_{\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}}\) remains constant at a given temperature. For the solid-liquid equilibrium \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\), the two phases coexist at a fixed melting point at constant pressure. For the dissolution of solid sugar in water, the concentration of sugar in the saturated solution is constant at a given temperature. For the dissolution of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) gas in water, Henry's law gives a constant ratio \(\frac{[\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{aq})]}{[\mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})]}\) at a given temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-1, C-4, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q02 - Common substances and their pH values

questiontext.text:
Match the common fluids with their characteristic \(\mathrm{pH}\) values at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\).

List I (Fluid)List II (\(\mathrm{pH}\))
(A) Gastric juice(1) \(10\)
(B) Human blood(2) \(5.0\)
(C) Milk of magnesia(3) \(\sim 1.2\)
(D) Black coffee(4) \(7.4\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aqueous biological and everyday fluids span the \(\mathrm{pH}\) scale from strongly acidic (\(\mathrm{pH} < 7\)) to basic (\(\mathrm{pH} > 7\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Fluid
Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid and is strongly acidic with a \(\mathrm{pH}\) of approximately \(1.2\). Human blood is slightly basic and tightly buffered at \(\mathrm{pH} = 7.4\). Milk of magnesia is an antacid suspension of \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) with \(\mathrm{pH} = 10\). Black coffee is mildly acidic with \(\mathrm{pH} = 5.0\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-3, B-4, C-1, and D-2.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q03 - Conjugate acids and conjugate bases

questiontext.text:
Match each Brönsted-Lowry species with its corresponding conjugate partner.

List I (Species and Role)List II (Conjugate Partner)
(A) Conjugate base of \(\mathrm{HF}\)(1) \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\)
(B) Conjugate base of \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\)(2) \(\mathrm{F}^-\)
(C) Conjugate acid of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)(3) \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\)
(D) Conjugate acid of \(\mathrm{HCOO}^-\)(4) \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A conjugate base has one fewer proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) than its parent Brönsted acid, whereas a conjugate acid has one extra proton compared to its parent Brönsted base.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pair
Removing one \(\mathrm{H}^+\) from \(\mathrm{HF}\) yields \(\mathrm{F}^-\). Removing one \(\mathrm{H}^+\) from \(\mathrm{HCO}_3^-\) yields \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\). Adding one \(\mathrm{H}^+\) to \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) yields \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\). Adding one \(\mathrm{H}^+\) to \(\mathrm{HCOO}^-\) yields \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-4, C-1, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q04 - Equilibrium constants for modified chemical equations

questiontext.text:
Given that the equilibrium constant for the reaction \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\) is \(K_c\), match the modified chemical equations with their equilibrium constants at the same temperature.

List I (Chemical Equation)List II (Equilibrium Constant)
(A) \(c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D} \rightleftharpoons a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B}\)(1) \(K_c^n\)
(B) \(na\mathrm{A} + nb\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons nc\mathrm{C} + nd\mathrm{D}\)(2) \(K_c^{1/2}\)
(C) \(\frac{1}{2}a\mathrm{A} + \frac{1}{2}b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}c\mathrm{C} + \frac{1}{2}d\mathrm{D}\)(3) \(\frac{1}{K_c^n}\)
(D) \(nc\mathrm{C} + nd\mathrm{D} \rightleftharpoons na\mathrm{A} + nb\mathrm{B}\)(4) \(\frac{1}{K_c}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
For \(a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D}\), \(K_c = \frac{[\mathrm{C}]^c[\mathrm{D}]^d}{[\mathrm{A}]^a[\mathrm{B}]^b}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Temperature is constant, and all concentrations are equilibrium molarities.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Reversing a balanced equation inverts its equilibrium constant, and multiplying all stoichiometric coefficients by a factor \(m\) raises the equilibrium constant to the power \(m\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Reversing the equation to \(c\mathrm{C} + d\mathrm{D} \rightleftharpoons a\mathrm{A} + b\mathrm{B}\) gives \(\frac{1}{K_c}\). Multiplying the forward equation by \(n\) gives \(K_c^n\). Multiplying the forward equation by \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives \(K_c^{1/2}\). Reversing the equation and multiplying by \(n\) both inverts and raises to the \(n\)-th power, giving \(\frac{1}{K_c^n}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are A-4, B-1, C-2, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q05 - Relationship between Kp and Kc for gaseous reactions

questiontext.text:
Match each equilibrium reaction with its correct relation between \(K_p\) and \(K_c\) (or partial pressure) at temperature \(T\).

List I (Reaction)List II (Relation)
(A) \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\)(1) \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\)(2) \(K_p = K_c(RT)\)
(C) \(\mathrm{PCl}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_3(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(3) \(K_p = K_c\)
(D) \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(4) \(K_p = p_{\mathrm{CO}_2}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four equilibrium reactions involving gases and solids at temperature \(T\) are given.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(\Delta n\) is the change in the number of moles of gaseous products minus gaseous reactants. Pure solids have constant concentration and do not appear in \(K_p\) or \(K_c\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta n = 2 - 2 = 0\), so \(K_p = K_c\). For \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta n = 2 - 4 = -2\), so \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}\). For \(\mathrm{PCl}_5(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{PCl}_3(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta n = 2 - 1 = 1\), so \(K_p = K_c(RT)\). For the heterogeneous equilibrium \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})\), only gaseous \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) contributes, so \(K_p = p_{\mathrm{CO}_2}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are A-3, B-1, C-2, and D-4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q06 - Equilibrium constant magnitude and reaction extent

questiontext.text:
Match the conditions involving equilibrium constant \(K_c\) and reaction quotient \(Q_c\) with their chemical interpretations.

List I (Condition)List II (Interpretation)
(A) \(K_c > 10^3\)(1) Appreciable concentrations of both reactants and products
(B) \(K_c < 10^{-3}\)(2) Reaction proceeds nearly to completion; products predominate
(C) \(10^{-3} \le K_c \le 10^3\)(3) Reaction mixture is at equilibrium; no net reaction
(D) \(Q_c = K_c\)(4) Reaction proceeds rarely; reactants predominate

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The numerical magnitude of \(K_c\) reflects the extent of a reaction at equilibrium, while comparing \(Q_c\) with \(K_c\) indicates whether the system is at equilibrium.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
When \(K_c > 10^3\), products strongly predominate and the reaction proceeds nearly to completion. When \(K_c < 10^{-3}\), reactants predominate and the reaction proceeds rarely. When \(K_c\) lies between \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^3\), appreciable concentrations of both reactants and products coexist. When \(Q_c = K_c\), the system has reached dynamic equilibrium and no net reaction occurs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-4, C-1, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q07 - Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant criteria

questiontext.text:
Match the thermodynamic conditions for a reversible reaction with their correct implications.

List I (Thermodynamic Condition)List II (Implication)
(A) \(\Delta G < 0\)(1) Equilibrium constant \(K > 1\)
(B) \(\Delta G > 0\)(2) Reaction is at equilibrium
(C) \(\Delta G = 0\)(3) Forward reaction is non-spontaneous
(D) \(\Delta G^\circ < 0\)(4) Forward reaction is spontaneous

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The spontaneity of a reaction at any instant is governed by \(\Delta G\), whereas the position of equilibrium is governed by the standard Gibbs energy change \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Condition
When \(\Delta G < 0\), the forward reaction is spontaneous. When \(\Delta G > 0\), the forward reaction is non-spontaneous and the reverse reaction proceeds. When \(\Delta G = 0\), no free energy remains to drive the reaction and the system is at equilibrium. When \(\Delta G^\circ < 0\), \(-\Delta G^\circ / RT > 0\), so \(K = e^{-\Delta G^\circ / RT} > 1\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-4, B-3, C-2, and D-1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q08 - Le Chatelier principle and pressure or catalyst

questiontext.text:
Match each equilibrium disturbance with its effect on the chemical system.

List I (Equilibrium and Disturbance)List II (Effect)
(A) Increasing pressure on \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\)(1) Equilibrium shifts in backward direction
(B) Increasing pressure on \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})\)(2) Equilibrium shifts in forward direction
(C) Increasing pressure on \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\)(3) Increases forward and reverse rates equally; no shift
(D) Adding a catalyst to \(2\mathrm{SO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO}_3(\mathrm{g})\)(4) Composition remains unaffected (\(\Delta n = 0\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Le Chatelier's principle, increasing pressure by decreasing volume shifts a gaseous equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas, while a catalyst lowers the activation energy of both forward and reverse reactions equally.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each System
In \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\), \(4\;\mathrm{mol}\) of gas form \(2\;\mathrm{mol}\) of gas, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium forward. In \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CaO}(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g})\), gaseous moles increase from \(0\) to \(1\), so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium backward. In \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\), \(\Delta n = 2 - 2 = 0\), so pressure changes do not affect the equilibrium composition. Adding a catalyst to \(2\mathrm{SO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{SO}_3(\mathrm{g})\) increases both forward and reverse rates equally without shifting the equilibrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-1, C-4, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q09 - Lewis acids and Lewis bases classification

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical species with their electronic behaviour according to the Lewis concept of acids and bases.

List I (Species)List II (Lewis Behaviour)
(A) \(\mathrm{BF}_3\)(1) Anion that donates an electron lone pair (Lewis base)
(B) \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)(2) Electron-deficient molecule that accepts an electron pair (Lewis acid)
(C) \(\mathrm{H}^+\)(3) Neutral molecule that donates a lone pair of electrons (Lewis base)
(D) \(\mathrm{F}^-\)(4) Bare proton that accepts a lone pair of electrons (Lewis acid)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Lewis theory, an acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a base is an electron-pair donor.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
\(\mathrm{BF}_3\) is an electron-deficient molecule lacking a proton, yet it acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair. \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has a lone pair on nitrogen and acts as a Lewis base by donating it. \(\mathrm{H}^+\) is a bare proton with an empty orbital, acting as a Lewis acid. \(\mathrm{F}^-\) is an anion with four lone pairs and acts as a Lewis base by donating one lone pair.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-3, C-4, and D-1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q10 - Salt hydrolysis and aqueous solution pH

questiontext.text:
Match the aqueous salt solutions with their \(\mathrm{pH}\) behaviour at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\).

List I (Salt)List II (\(\mathrm{pH}\) Behaviour)
(A) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)(1) Acidic (\(\mathrm{pH} < 7\))
(B) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\)(2) Neutral (\(\mathrm{pH} = 7\))
(C) \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\)(3) \(\mathrm{pH} = 7 + \frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_b)\)
(D) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONH}_4\)(4) Basic (\(\mathrm{pH} > 7\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The \(\mathrm{pH}\) of an aqueous salt solution depends on whether the cation and/or anion undergo hydrolysis with water.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Salt
\(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is formed from a strong acid (\(\mathrm{HCl}\)) and strong base (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)); its ions only hydrate and do not hydrolyse, giving \(\mathrm{pH} = 7\). \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\) is formed from a weak acid and strong base; \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-\) hydrolyses to produce \(\mathrm{OH}^-\), giving \(\mathrm{pH} > 7\). \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\) is formed from a strong acid and weak base; \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) hydrolyses to produce \(\mathrm{H}^+\), giving \(\mathrm{pH} < 7\). \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONH}_4\) is formed from a weak acid and weak base, so its \(\mathrm{pH}\) is given by \(7 + \frac{1}{2}(\mathrm{p}K_a - \mathrm{p}K_b)\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-4, C-1, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q11 - Ionization constants Ka of weak acids

questiontext.text:
Match the weak acids with their ionization constants \(K_a\) at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) based on their relative acid strengths.

List I (Weak Acid)List II (\(K_a\) at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\))
(A) Hydrofluoric acid (\(\mathrm{HF}\))(1) \(1.74 \times 10^{-5}\)
(B) Acetic acid (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\))(2) \(4.9 \times 10^{-10}\)
(C) Hypochlorous acid (\(\mathrm{HClO}\))(3) \(3.5 \times 10^{-4}\)
(D) Hydrocyanic acid (\(\mathrm{HCN}\))(4) \(3.0 \times 10^{-8}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A larger value of the acid ionization constant \(K_a\) corresponds to a stronger acid.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Acid
Among these four weak acids, \(\mathrm{HF}\) is the strongest with \(K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-4}\). Acetic acid (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\)) is next with \(K_a = 1.74 \times 10^{-5}\). Hypochlorous acid (\(\mathrm{HClO}\)) is weaker with \(K_a = 3.0 \times 10^{-8}\), and hydrocyanic acid (\(\mathrm{HCN}\)) is the weakest among them with \(K_a = 4.9 \times 10^{-10}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-3, B-1, C-4, and D-2.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q12 - Solubility product expressions in terms of molar solubility

questiontext.text:
Match each sparingly soluble ionic salt with its solubility product constant \(K_{sp}\) expressed in terms of its molar solubility \(S\) in pure water (assuming no hydrolysis).

List I (Salt)List II (\(K_{sp}\) in terms of \(S\))
(A) \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\)(1) \(27S^4\)
(B) \(\mathrm{Ag}_2\mathrm{CrO}_4\)(2) \(S^2\)
(C) \(\mathrm{Al(OH)}_3\)(3) \(6912S^7\)
(D) \(\mathrm{Zr}_3(\mathrm{PO}_4)_4\)(4) \(4S^3\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four sparingly soluble salts with different cation-to-anion stoichiometries are given, each with molar solubility \(S\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Hydrolysis of ions is neglected, and the solution is saturated.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a general salt \(M_x X_y(\mathrm{s}) \rightleftharpoons xM^{p+}(\mathrm{aq}) + yX^{q-}(\mathrm{aq})\), \(K_{sp} = (xS)^x (yS)^y = x^x y^y S^{x+y}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\) (\(x=1, y=1\)): \(K_{sp} = (S)(S) = S^2\). For \(\mathrm{Ag}_2\mathrm{CrO}_4\) (\(x=2, y=1\)): \(K_{sp} = (2S)^2(S) = 4S^3\). For \(\mathrm{Al(OH)}_3\) (\(x=1, y=3\)): \(K_{sp} = (S)(3S)^3 = 27S^4\). For \(\mathrm{Zr}_3(\mathrm{PO}_4)_4\) (\(x=3, y=4\)): \(K_{sp} = (3S)^3(4S)^4 = 27 \times 256 S^7 = 6912S^7\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are A-2, B-4, C-1, and D-3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q13 - Buffer solutions and their pH values

questiontext.text:
Match each buffer mixture at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) with its resulting \(\mathrm{pH}\) value.

List I (Buffer Mixture)List II (\(\mathrm{pH}\))
(A) Equimolar \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) (\(\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.76\)) and \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\)(1) \(8.95\)
(B) Equimolar \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{OH}\) and \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(\mathrm{p}K_a\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+ = 9.25\))(2) \(4.76\)
(C) \(0.05\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) (\(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\)) and \(0.05\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-\)(3) \(9.25\)
(D) \(0.10\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NH}_3\) (\(\mathrm{p}K_b = 4.75\)) and \(0.20\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\)(4) \(4.74\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four buffer mixtures at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) with specified acid/base and conjugate salt concentrations and \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) or \(\mathrm{p}K_b\) values.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Henderson-Hasselbalch approximations apply, and \(\mathrm{p}K_w = 14\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For an acidic buffer, \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\left(\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]}\right)\). For a basic buffer, \(\mathrm{pOH} = \mathrm{p}K_b + \log\left(\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Base}]}\right)\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 14 - \mathrm{pOH}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For equimolar \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\), \(\frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} = 1\), so \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a = 4.76\). For equimolar \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{OH}\) and \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\), \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a(\mathrm{NH}_4^+) = 9.25\). For \(0.05\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) (\(K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\)) and \(0.05\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-\), \([\mathrm{H}^+] = K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}\;\mathrm{M}\), so \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(1.8 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.74\). For \(0.10\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(0.20\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\), \(\mathrm{pOH} = 4.75 + \log\left(\frac{0.20}{0.10}\right) = 4.75 + 0.30 = 5.05\), giving \(\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 5.05 = 8.95\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are A-2, B-3, C-4, and D-1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q14 - pH of strong and weak electrolyte solutions

questiontext.text:
Match each aqueous solution at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) with its correct \(\mathrm{pH}\) value.

List I (Aqueous Solution)List II (\(\mathrm{pH}\))
(A) \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\)(1) \(6.98\)
(B) \(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NaOH}\)(2) \(4.50\)
(C) \(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\)(3) \(2.00\)
(D) \(0.10\;\mathrm{M}\) monobasic weak acid (\(K_a = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\))(4) \(10.00\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four aqueous solutions at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\) (\(K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\)) are given.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(\mathrm{HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) dissociate completely; for the very dilute \(10^{-8}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\) solution, auto-ionization of water must be included.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+]\), \(\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14\), and for a weak monobasic acid with \(c \gg [\mathrm{H}^+]\), \([\mathrm{H}^+] \approx \sqrt{K_a c}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(10^{-2}) = 2.00\). For \(1.0 \times 10^{-4}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{NaOH}\), \(\mathrm{pOH} = 4.00\), so \(\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 4.00 = 10.00\). For \(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{M}\;\mathrm{HCl}\), solving \((10^{-8} + x)x = 10^{-14}\) gives \(x = [\mathrm{OH}^-] = 9.5 \times 10^{-8}\;\mathrm{M}\), so \(\mathrm{pOH} = 7.02\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = 6.98\). For \(0.10\;\mathrm{M}\) weak acid with \(K_a = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\), \([\mathrm{H}^+] = \sqrt{1.0 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.10} = \sqrt{10^{-9}} = 10^{-4.5}\;\mathrm{M}\), giving \(\mathrm{pH} = 4.50\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The correct pairings are A-3, B-4, C-1, and D-2.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q15 - Solubility product constants of silver halides and HgS

questiontext.text:
Match the sparingly soluble salts with their solubility product constants \(K_{sp}\) at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\).

List I (Salt)List II (\(K_{sp}\) at \(298\;\mathrm{K}\))
(A) \(\mathrm{AgCl}\)(1) \(4.0 \times 10^{-53}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{AgBr}\)(2) \(1.8 \times 10^{-10}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{AgI}\)(3) \(8.3 \times 10^{-17}\)
(D) \(\mathrm{HgS}\)(4) \(5.0 \times 10^{-13}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For \(1:1\) electrolytes, a smaller \(K_{sp}\) value corresponds to lower solubility in pure water.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Salt
Among the silver halides, solubility decreases from \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) to \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) to \(\mathrm{AgI}\): \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) has \(K_{sp} = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}\), \(\mathrm{AgBr}\) has \(K_{sp} = 5.0 \times 10^{-13}\), and \(\mathrm{AgI}\) has \(K_{sp} = 8.3 \times 10^{-17}\). Mercuric sulphide (\(\mathrm{HgS}\)) is extremely insoluble with \(K_{sp} = 4.0 \times 10^{-53}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-2, B-4, C-3, and D-1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_MATCH_Q16 - Factors governing acid strength and common ion effect

questiontext.text:
Match each chemical trend or observation with its governing principle.

List I (Trend / Observation)List II (Governing Principle)
(A) Acid strength: \(\mathrm{HF} \ll \mathrm{HCl} \ll \mathrm{HBr} \ll \mathrm{HI}\)(1) Suppression of weak acid ionization by common ion effect
(B) Acid strength: \(\mathrm{CH}_4 < \mathrm{NH}_3 < \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} < \mathrm{HF}\)(2) Precipitation of ionic salt when \(Q_{sp} > K_{sp}\) due to increased \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) activity
(C) Adding \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\) to \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) solution(3) Decreasing \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond strength down a group
(D) Passing \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas into saturated \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) solution(4) Increasing \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond polarity across a period

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acid strength depends on \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond strength down a group and \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond polarity across a period, while ionic equilibria respond to added common ions according to Le Chatelier's principle.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Observation
Down Group 17 (\(\mathrm{HF}\) to \(\mathrm{HI}\)), increasing halogen size weakens the \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{X}\) bond, so decreasing bond strength governs the increase in acidity. Across the second period (\(\mathrm{CH}_4\) to \(\mathrm{HF}\)), increasing electronegativity increases \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{A}\) bond polarity, which governs the increase in acidity. Adding \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\) supplies \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-\) ions and suppresses \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COOH}\) ionization via the common ion effect. Passing \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas into saturated \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) raises \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) activity so that \(Q_{sp} > K_{sp}\), precipitating pure \(\mathrm{NaCl}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are A-3, B-4, C-1, and D-2.
